== Threats to forest ecology ==

=== Deforestation ===
A significant threat to forest ecology is deforestation as it removes large areas of forest for timer and land development.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Devaraju |first1=N. |last2=Bala |first2=Govindasamy |last3=Modak |first3=Angshuman |date=2015-03-17 |title=Effects of large-scale deforestation on precipitation in the monsoon regions: Remote versus local effects |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |language=en |volume=112 |issue=11 |pages=3257–3262 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1423439112 |doi-access=free |pmid=25733889 |pmc=4371945 |bibcode=2015PNAS..112.3257D |issn=0027-8424}}</ref><ref name=":6">{{Cite web |last1=Franklin |first1=Alan |last2=Noon |first2=Barry |last3=George |first3=Luke |date=2002 |title=What is Habitat Fragmentation? |url=https://digitalcommons.usf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1658&context=sab |access-date=2026-03-26 |website=Digital Sommons}}</ref> As trees are cleared, forest habitat become fragmented into smaller patches, making it harder for forest dependent species to fines resources like shelter, food, and mates.<ref>https://www.seesouthernforests.org/case-studies/biological-consequences-fragmentation/#:~:text=Fragmentation%20is%20problematic%20because%20it,invasive%20species%2C%20such%20as%20kudzu.</ref><ref name=":6" /> This poorly impacts forest ecology as it declines biodiversity and disrupts ecosystem functions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Magrach |first1=Ainhoa |last2=Senior |first2=Rebecca A. |last3=Rogers |first3=Andrew |last4=Nurdin |first4=Deddy |last5=Benedick |first5=Suzan |last6=Laurance |first6=William F. |last7=Santamaria |first7=Luis |last8=Edwards |first8=David P. |date=2016-03-16 |title=Selective logging in tropical forests decreases the robustness of liana–tree interaction networks to the loss of host tree species |journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences |language=en |volume=283 |issue=1826 |article-number=20153008 |doi=10.1098/rspb.2015.3008 |issn=0962-8452 |pmc=4810863 |pmid=26936241 |bibcode=2016PBioS.28353008M }}</ref>

Likewise, agricultural activities transform forests into farmland and monocultures,<ref name=":6" /> introducing chemicals like fertilizers and pesticides that harm the soil.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Addison |first1=S. L. |last2=Smaill |first2=S. J. |last3=Garrett |first3=L. G. |last4=Wakelin |first4=S. === Approaches ===
[[Image: Redwood M D Vaden.jpg|thumb|right|[[Sequoia sempervirens|Redwood]] tree in northern California forest, where many trees are managed for preservation and longevity]]
Forests are studied at a number of organizational levels, from the individual [[organism]] to the ecosystem. However, as the term [[forest]] connotes an area inhabited by more than one [[organism]], forest ecology most often concentrates on the level of the [[Population (biology)|population]], [[community]] or ecosystem. Logically, [[tree]]s are an important component of forest research, but the wide variety of other life forms and [[abiotic components]] in most forests means that other elements, such as [[wildlife]] or [[soil]] [[nutrients]], are also crucial components.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dunson |first1=William A. |last2=Travis |first2=Joseph |date=1991 |title=The Role of Abiotic Factors in Community Organization |journal=The American Naturalist |volume=138 |issue=5 |pages=1067–1091 |doi=10.1086/285270 |jstor=2462508 |bibcode=1991ANat..138.1067D |issn=0003-0147}}</ref>

Forest ecology shares characteristics and methodological approaches with other areas of [[terrestrial plant]] ecology, however, the presence of trees makes forest ecosystems and their study unique in numerous ways due to the potential for a wide variety of forest structures created by the uniquely large size and height of trees compared with other terrestrial plants.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ehbrecht |first1=Martin |last2=Seidel |first2=Dominik |last3=Annighöfer |first3=Peter |last4=Kreft |first4=Holger |last5=Köhler |first5=Michael |last6=Zemp |first6=Delphine Clara |last7=Puettmann |first7=Klaus |last8=Nilus |first8=Reuben |last9=Babweteera |first9=Fred |last10=Willim |first10=Katharina |last11=Stiers |first11=Melissa |last12=Soto |first12=Daniel |last13=Boehmer |first13=Hans Juergen |last14=Fisichelli |first14=Nicholas |last15=Burnett |first15=Michael |date=2021-01-22 |title=Global patterns and climatic controls of forest structural complexity |journal=Nature Communications |language=en |volume=12 |issue=1 |page=519 |doi=10.1038/s41467-020-20767-z |pmid=33483481 |pmc=7822964 |bibcode=2021NatCo..12..519E |issn=2041-1723}}</ref>

The emergence of [[machine learning]](ML) has allowed for new methods of approaching forest ecology, as it can process larger and more complex data. Since the 1990s, machine learning is increasingly used to improve the accuracy of [[Species distribution modelling|species distribution models]], predict [[Carbon cycle|carbon flux]], and in hazard assessment procedures.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last1=Liu |first1=Zelin |last2=Peng |first2=Changhui |last3=Work |first3=Timothy |last4=Candau |first4=Jean-Noel |last5=DesRochers |first5=Annie |last6=Kneeshaw |first6=Daniel |date=2018 |title=Application of machine-learning methods in forest ecology: recent progress and future challenges |url=https://cdnsciencepub.com/doi/10.1139/er-2018-0034 |journal=Environmental Reviews |language=en |volume=26 |issue=4 |pages=339–350 |doi=10.1139/er-2018-0034 |bibcode=2018EnvRv..26..339L |hdl=1807/92561 |issn=1181-8700}}</ref> Drones are also heavily used in forest ecology research.<ref name=":5" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bygjymi |first1=Xhulia |last2=Begu |first2=Enkela |last3=Lloci |first3=Dritan |last4=Sinjari |first4=Sonila |last5=Hanxhari |first5=Romeo |date=2025 |title=The Use of Drone/Uav Technology in Precision Forestry. === Climate Change and Carbon Cycling ===

== Community diversity and complexity ==
[[File:Overall decline in a forest-specialist index for 268 forest vertebrate species (455 populations), 1970–2014.svg|thumb|upright=1.35|Overall decline in a forest-specialist index for 268 forest vertebrate species (455 populations), 1970–2014, from the [[Food and Agriculture Organization]] publication The State of the World's Forests 2020. Since trees can grow larger than other plant life-forms, there is the potential for a wide variety of forest structures (or physiognomies). The infinite number of possible spatial arrangements of trees of varying size and species makes for a highly intricate and diverse micro-environment in which environmental variables such as [[solar radiation]], temperature, [[relative humidity]], and [[wind speed]] can vary considerably over large and small distances.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Schnabel |first1=Florian |last2=Beugnon |first2=Rémy |last3=Yang |first3=Bo |last4=Richter |first4=Ronny |last5=Eisenhauer |first5=Nico |last6=Huang |first6=Yuanyuan |last7=Liu |first7=Xiaojuan |last8=Wirth |first8=Christian |last9=Cesarz |first9=Simone |last10=Fichtner |first10=Andreas |last11=Perles-Garcia |first11=Maria D. |last12=Hähn |first12=Georg J. A. |last13=Härdtle |first13=Werner |last14=Kunz |first14=Matthias |last15=Castro Izaguirre |first15=Nadia C. |date=March 2025 |title=Tree Diversity Increases Forest Temperature Buffering via Enhancing Canopy Density and Structural Diversity |journal=Ecology Letters |volume=28 |issue=3 |article-number=e70096 |doi=10.1111/ele.70096 |issn=1461-0248 |pmc=11928777 |pmid=40119529 |bibcode=2025EcolL..28E0096S }}</ref> In addition, an important proportion of a forest ecosystem's [[biomass (ecology)|biomass]] is often underground, where soil structure, [[water quality]] and quantity, and levels of various soil nutrients can vary greatly.<ref>James P. Kimmins. 2004</ref> Thus, forests are often highly [[heterogeneous]] environments compared to other [[terrestrial plant]] communities. This heterogeneity in turn can enable great biodiversity of species of both plants and animals. Some structures, such as tree ferns may be keystone species for a diverse range of other species.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Fountain-Jones | first1=Nicholas M. | last2=McQuillan | first2=Peter B. | last3=Grove | first3=Simon | title=Beetle communities associated with the tree fern ''Dicksonia antarctica'' Labill. A number of factors within the forest affect biodiversity; primary factors enhancing wildlife abundance and biodiversity was the presence of diverse tree species within the forest and the absence of [[even aged timber management]].<ref>Philip Joseph Burton. 2003</ref> For example, the [[wild turkey]] thrives when uneven heights and [[Canopy (biology)|canopy]] variations exist and its numbers are diminished by even aged timber management.

=== Tropical forests ===
[[File:Cuniculus_paca.jpg|thumb|Paca the South American rodent species that has shared features with the African chevrotain due to convergent evolution.]]
[[File:Indian_spotted_chevrotain_Moschiola_indica_Mouse_deer_from_the_Anaimalai_hills_DSC9927_03.jpg|thumb|The African chevrotain an ungulate that shares convergently evolved features with the South American paca.]]
[[Tropical forest|Tropical forests]] are some of the most [[Biodiversity|diverse]] ecosystems in the world.<ref name=":3">{{Cite book |last1=Ehrlich |first1=Paul R. |title=The science of ecology |last2=Roughgarden |first2=Joan |date=1987 |publisher=Macmillan ; Collier Macmillan |isbn=978-0-02-331700-2 |location=New York : London}}</ref> Although there are many different tree species present per acre of forest, many share similar appearances due to the similar environmental pressures.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite book |title=The International book of the forest |date=1981 |publisher=Simon and Schuster |isbn=978-0-671-41004-9 |location=New York}}</ref> Some of these shared traits, possessed by many tropical trees, include thick and leathery leaves that are elongated and ovular with [[Midrib|mid-ribs]] and [[Drip-tip|drip-tips]].<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":2" /> These adaptations help to quickly drain water from the leaves, likely to help prevent [[algae]] or [[lichen]] growth<ref name=":3" /> and prevent water reflecting the sunlight or restricting [[transpiration]].<ref name=":2" /> Commonly, tropical trees have large [[Buttress root|buttress roots]] on larger trees, and [[stilt roots]] on mid-sized trees which help support their tall and vertical structures in the shallow and moist soil.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":2" /> Tropical forests grow very densely due to the heavy rainfall and year-round growing season. This creates competition for light which causes many trees to grow very tall, blocking out most or all of the light from reaching the [[forest floor]].<ref name=":3" /> Because of this, the [[Canopy (biology)|canopy]] exhibits distinct stratified layers from the tallest trees to the tightly packed midstory trees below.<ref name=":3" /> Due to low light on the forest floor, there is a diverse population of [[Epiphyte|epiphytes]], a type of plant that grows on the canopy trees, rather than soil, to access better light. Many [[Vine|vines]] use a similar tactic, however they root in the ground, growing up the trees to reach light.<ref name=":3" /> The [[fauna]] in tropical forests also show many unique adaptations to fill various [[Ecological niche|niches]]. These adaptations are possessed by different species depending on where they are located.<ref name=":3" /> For example, there are similar looking animals in the rainforests of South America and Africa that share ecological niches, however the mammals from South America are [[Rodent|rodents]] while the African ones are [[Ungulate|ungulates]]. This clearly demonstrates the [[convergent evolution]] between species found in tropical forest environments.<ref name=":3" />

=== Coniferous forests ===
[[Conifer|Conifers]] have unique traits that make them especially adapted to harsh conditions, including cold, drought, wind, and snow.<ref name=":2" /> Their leaves have a [[wax]] coating and are filled with [[resin]] to help prevent moisture loss, this makes them unpalatable to animals and slow to [[Decomposition|decompose]]. This [[leaf litter]] creates an acidic forest floor that is distinct to coniferous forests.<ref name=":2" /> Because of the types of leaves possessed by conifers, they face the problem of soil nutrient loss; this problem is solved through [[Mycorrhizal network|mycorrhizal symbiosis]] with [[Fungus|fungi]] that help transport the limited nutrients to the trees in exchange for [[Glucose|sugars]].<ref name=":2" /> Some conifers are incapable of surviving without mycorrhizal fungi.<ref name=":2" /> The majority of conifers are also [[evergreen]], allowing them to take advantage of the short growing seasons of their respective environments.<ref name=":2" /> Their thin tapered structure helps them to withstand strong winds without being blown over.<ref name=":2" /> The stereotypically cone shape of conifers helps prevent large quantities of snow from building up on their branches and breaking them.<ref name=":3" /> Due to the harsh environments that coniferous forests are commonly found, the diversity is limited in both plant and animal species. The colder climates limit the number of [[Reptile|reptilian]] and [[amphibian]] species that can survive.<ref name=":2" /> The species more commonly found in coniferous forests are [[Mammal|mammals]], including large [[Herbivore|herbivores]] such as [[moose]] and [[elk]], [[Predation|predators]] like [[Bear|bears]] and [[Wolf|wolves]], along with a few smaller species like [[Rabbit|rabbits]], [[Fox|foxes]], and [[mink]]. There are also a variety of [[migratory bird]] species and some [[Bird of prey|birds of prey]] such as [[Owl|owls]] and [[Hawk|hawks]].<ref name=":2" /> Coniferous forests contain a variety of valuable [[Pulp (paper)|pulp]] and [[lumber]] trees making them some of the most [[economically]] important ecosystems.<ref name=":2" /> They have also been historically sought for the [[fur trade]] due to the animals species that inhabit them.<ref name=":2" />

== Ecological interactions ==

=== Plant-plant interactions ===
In forests, trees and shrubs often serve as [[nurse plants]] that facilitate the establishment and seedling growth of understory plants. The forest canopy protects young understory plants from extremes of temperature and dry conditions.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Martinkova |first1=Zdenka |last2=Honek |first2=Alois |last3=Pekar |first3=Stano |title=The Role of Nurse Plants in Facilitating the Germination of Dandelion (Taraxacum officinale) Seeds |journal=Weed Science |date=2014 |volume=62 |issue=3|pages=474–482 |doi=10.1614/WS-D-13-00162.1 |bibcode=2014WeedS..62..474M |s2cid=85658841 }}</ref> 

=== Mycorrhizal symbiosis ===
[[File:Positive_effects_of_arbuscular_mycorrhizal_(AM)_colonization.png|thumb|The benefits of mycorrhizal fungi interacting with plant roots to improve nutrient absorption among other benefits compared to a plant without this symbiotic relationship.]]
{{main|Mycorrhizal network}}

An important interaction in forest ecosystems is the mycorrhizal network, which consists of fungi and plants that share [[Symbiosis|symbiotic]] relationships.<ref name=":02">{{cite journal |last1=Van der Heijden |first1=Marcel G. A. |last2=Horton |first2=Thomas R. |date=2009 |title=Socialism in Soil? the Importance of Mycorrhizal Fungal Networks for Facilitation in Natural Ecosystems |journal=Journal of Ecology |volume=97 |issue=6}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Agathokleous |first1=E. |last2=Feng |first2=Z. |last3=Oksanen |first3=E. |last4=Sicard |first4=P. |last5=Wang |first5=Q. |last6=Saitanis |first6=C. J. |last7=Araminiene |first7=V. |last8=Blande |first8=J. D. |last9=Hayes |first9=F. |last10=Calatayud |first10=V. |last11=Domingos |first11=M. |last12=Veresoglou |first12=S. D. |last13=Peñuelas |first13=J. |last14=Wardle |first14=D. A. |last15=De Marco |first15=A. |last16=Li |first16=Z. |last17=Harmens |first17=H. |last18=Yuan |first18=X. |last19=Vitale |first19=M. |last20=Paoletti |first20=E. |date=12 August 2020 |title=Ozone affects plant, insect, and soil microbial communities: A threat to terrestrial ecosystems and biodiversity |journal=Science Advances |volume=6 |issue=33 |article-number=eabc1176 |doi=10.1126/sciadv.abc1176 |pmid=32851188 |pmc=7423369 |bibcode=2020SciA....6.1176A }}</ref> Mycorrhizal networks have been shown to increase the uptake of important nutrients, especially ones which disperse slowly into the soil like [[Phosphorus cycle|phosphorus]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |title=Environmental restoration: science and strategies for restoring the Earth |date=1990 |publisher=Island Press |isbn=978-0-933280-94-6 |editor-last=Berger |editor-first=John J. |location=Washington, D.C. |editor-last2=Restoring the Earth (Organization) |editor-last3=University of California, Berkeley |editor-last4=University of California, Berkeley |editor-last5=San Francisco Bay Conservation and Development Commission}}</ref> The fine [[hypha]] of the [[mycelium]] is able to reach farther into the soil than the roots of the plant, allowing it to better access phosphorus and water.<ref name=":1" /> The mycorrhizal network can also transport water and nutrients between plants.<ref name="Binghman20112">{{cite journal |last1=Bingham |first1=Marcus A. |last2=Simard |first2=Suzanne W. |year=2011 |title=Do mycorrhizal network benefits to survival and growth of interior Douglas-fir seedlings increase with soil moisture stress? === Ecological potential of forest species ===
The ecological potential of a particular species is a measure of its capacity to effectively compete in a given geographical area, ahead of other species, as they all try to occupy a natural space. For some areas it has been quantified, as for instance by Hans-Jürgen Otto, for central Europe.<ref>{{cite book|last=Otto|first=Hans-Jürgen|title=Écologie Forestière|year=1998|publisher=Institut pour le Développement Forestier|location=Paris|isbn=978-2-904740-65-7|language=fr}}</ref> He takes three groups of parameters:

# Related to site requirements: Tolerance to low temperatures, tolerance to dry climate, frugality.
# Specific qualities: [[Shade tolerance]], height growth, stability, longevity, regeneration capacity.
# Specific risks: Resistance to late freezing, resistance to wind/ice storm, resistance to fire, resistance to biotic agents.

Every parameter is scored between 0 and 5 for each considered species, and then a global mean value calculated. A value above 3.5 is considered high, below 3.0 low, and intermediate for those in between. In this study ''[[Fagus sylvatica]]'' has a score of 3.82, ''[[Fraxinus excelsior]]'' 3.08 and ''[[Juglans regia]]'' 2.92; and are examples of the three categories.

=== Competition ===
Forest ecosystem interactions consist of not only symbiotic relationships, but also competition. Competition can either be in forms of [[Intraspecific competition|intraspecific]] or [[Interspecific competition|interspecific]] competition.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Interspecific Competition - an overview {{!}} ScienceDirect Topics|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/interspecific-competition|access-date=2026-04-05|website=www.sciencedirect.com}}</ref> Intraspecific competition can occur between members of the same species for resources, whereas interspecific competition occurs between different species in a population.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Interspecific Competition - an overview {{!}} ScienceDirect Topics|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/interspecific-competition|access-date=2026-04-05|website=www.sciencedirect.com}}</ref> For example, in order to fulfil nutritional needs decomposing organic matter in soils is a sought after resource by plants, microbes and fungi.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fontaine|first1=Sébastien|last2=Mariotti|first2=André|last3=Abbadie|first3=Luc|date=2003-06-01|title=The priming effect of organic matter: a question of microbial competition?|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0038071703001238|journal=Soil Biology and Biochemistry|volume=35|issue=6|pages=837–843|doi=10.1016/S0038-0717(03)00123-8|bibcode=2003SBiBi..35..837F |issn=0038-0717}}</ref> Invasive species in forest ecosystems also play a role in interspecific competition.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Invasive Species - an overview {{!}} ScienceDirect Topics|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/pharmacology-toxicology-and-pharmaceutical-science/invasive-species|access-date=2026-04-05|website=www.sciencedirect.com}}</ref> They often compete with native species for resources and may conquer these resources successfully due to low intraspecific competition.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Woo|first1=Sohyun|last2=Kim|first2=Tae-Min|last3=Kim|first3=Yousuk|last4=Jeong|first4=Seorin|last5=Kim|first5=Eunsuk|date=October 2024|title=Inter- and Intraspecific Competition in Invasive Lactuca serriola and Co-Occurring Weedy Plant Species|journal=Ecology and Evolution|volume=14|issue=10|article-number=e70496|doi=10.1002/ece3.70496|issn=2045-7758|pmc=11522139|pmid=39478980 |bibcode=2024EcoEv..1470496W }}</ref> The [[hemlock woolly adelgid]] and the [[emerald ash borer]] are examples of well known invasive species that colonize an area and create disturbances in forest ecology by killing off host trees and decreasing the vegetation in a forest as a result.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Environmental and Ecological Impacts {{!}} National Invasive Species Information Center|url=https://www.invasivespeciesinfo.gov/subject/environmental-and-ecological-impacts|access-date=2026-04-05|website=www.invasivespeciesinfo.gov|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Canada|first=Natural Resources|date=2013-10-24|title=Emerald ash borer (factsheet)|url=https://natural-resources.canada.ca/forests-forestry/insects-disturbances/emerald-ash-borer-factsheet|access-date=2026-04-05|website=natural-resources.canada.ca}}</ref>

== Matter and energy flows ==

=== Energy flux ===
[[File:RockyPointTrailAsFirebreak.jpg|thumb|upright=1.1|Forest ecologists are interested in the effects of large disturbances, such as [[wildfire]]s. [[Montana]], United States.]]
Forests accumulate large amounts of standing biomass, and many are capable of accumulating it at high rates, i.e. they are highly productive. Such high levels of biomass and tall vertical structures represent large stores of [[potential energy]] that can be converted to [[kinetic energy]] under the right circumstances.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Running |first1=S. W. |title=Science |url=https://www.science.org/action/cookieAbsent |access-date=2026-03-30 |journal=Science |date=2008 |volume=321 |issue=5889 |pages=652–653 |language=en |doi=10.1126/science.1159607 |pmid=18669853 }}</ref>

The world's forests contain about 606 [[Metric ton|gigatonnes]] of living biomass (above- and below-ground) and 59 gigatonnes of dead wood.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Global Forest Resources Assessment 2020 – Key findings|publisher=FAO|year=2020|isbn=978-92-5-132581-0|location=Rome|doi=10.4060/ca8753en|s2cid=130116768}}</ref>

Two such conversions of great importance are [[wildfires|fires]] and [[windthrow|treefall]]s, both of which radically alter forest structure and ecosystem processes and the physical environment where they occur.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bowd |first1=Elle |last2=Lindenmayer |first2=David |date=January 2026 |title=Setting the benchmark: Patterns of forest structure after wildfire in temperate, montane forests across a multi-century chronosequence |url=https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1365-2745.70227 |journal=Journal of Ecology |language=en |volume=114 |issue=1 |article-number=e70227 |doi=10.1111/1365-2745.70227 |bibcode=2026JEcol.11470227B |issn=0022-0477}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Seidl |first1=Rupert |last2=Rammer |first2=Werner |last3=Spies |first3=Thomas A. |date=2014-12-01 |title=Disturbance legacies increase the resilience of forest ecosystem structure, composition, and functioning |journal=Ecological Applications: A Publication of the Ecological Society of America |volume=24 |issue=8 |pages=2063–2077 |doi=10.1890/14-0255.1 |issn=1051-0761 |pmc=4820056 |pmid=27053913 |bibcode=2014EcoAp..24.2063S }}</ref> Also, in forests of high productivity, the rapid growth of the trees themselves induces biome and environmental changes, although at a slower rate and lower intensity than relatively instantaneous [[disturbance (ecology)|disturbances]] such as fires.

=== Water ===
Forest trees store large amounts of water because of their large size and anatomical/physiological characteristics.  They are therefore important regulators of hydrological processes, especially those involving groundwater [[hydrology]] and local evaporation and [[Precipitation (meteorology)|rainfall/snowfall]] patterns.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Smerdon|first=Brian D|display-authors=etal|year=2009|title=An overview of the effects of forest management on ground water hydrology|url=http://forrex.org/sites/default/files/publications/jem_archive/ISS50/vol10_no1_art4.pdf|journal=BC Journal of Ecosystems and Management|volume=10|issue=1|pages=22–44|access-date=2016-11-21|archive-date=2016-11-22|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161122153621/http://forrex.org/sites/default/files/publications/jem_archive/ISS50/vol10_no1_art4.pdf}}</ref>

An estimated 399 million ha of forest is designated primarily for the protection of soil and water, an increase of 119 million ha since 1990.<ref name=":0" />

Thus, forest ecological studies are sometimes closely aligned with [[meteorology|meteorological]] and hydrological studies in regional ecosystem or resource planning studies. Perhaps more importantly the duff or [[leaf litter]] can form a major repository of water storage. When this litter is removed or compacted (through grazing or human overuse), erosion and flooding are exacerbated as well as deprivation of dry season water for forest organisms.

=== Death and regeneration ===
[[File:Cascades Regrowth after forest fire.jpg|thumb|upright=1.1|Forest regrowth after a forest fire, [[Cascade Range]], United States]]
Woody material, often referred to as [[coarse woody debris]], [[decomposition|decay]]s relatively slowly in many forests in comparison to most other [[organic matter|organic]] materials, due to a combination of environmental factors and wood chemistry (see [[lignin]]).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ganjegunte |first1=Girisha K |last2=Condron |first2=Leo M |last3=Clinton |first3=Peter W |last4=Davis |first4=Murray R |last5=Mahieu |first5=Nathalie |date=2004-01-23 |title=Decomposition and nutrient release from radiata pine (Pinus radiata) coarse woody debris |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378112703003323 |journal=Forest Ecology and Management |language=en |volume=187 |issue=2 |pages=197–211 |doi=10.1016/S0378-1127(03)00332-3 |bibcode=2004ForEM.187..197G |issn=0378-1127|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Trees growing in [[arid]] and/or cold environments do so especially slowly. Thus, tree trunks and branches can remain on the [[forest floor]] for long periods, affecting such things as wildlife [[habitat]], fire behaviour, and tree [[regeneration (biology)|regeneration]] processes.

Some trees leave behind eerie skeletons after death. In reality these deaths are actually very few compared to the amount of tree deaths that go unnoticed. Thousands of seedlings can be produced from a single tree but only a few can actually grow to maturity.<ref name="Tree Death: Cause and Consequence">{{Cite journal|date=1987|title=Competition and Tree Death|journal=BioScience |volume=37|pages=586–595|jstor=1310669|last1=Peet|first1=Robert K.|last2=Christensen|first2=Norman L.|issue=8|doi=10.2307/1310669}}</ref> Most of those deaths are caused from competition for light, water, or soil nutrients, this is called natural thinning. Singular deaths caused by natural thinning go unnoticed, but many deaths can help form forest ecosystems.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Swanson |first1=Mark E |last2=Franklin |first2=Jerry F |last3=Beschta |first3=Robert L |last4=Crisafulli |first4=Charles M |last5=DellaSala |first5=Dominick A |last6=Hutto |first6=Richard L |last7=Lindenmayer |first7=David B |last8=Swanson |first8=Frederick J |date=2011 |title=The forgotten stage of forest succession: early-successional ecosystems on forest sites |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1890/090157 |journal=Frontiers in Ecology and the Environment |language=en |volume=9 |issue=2 |pages=117–125 |doi=10.1890/090157 |bibcode=2011FrEE....9..117S |issn=1540-9309}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Luu |first1=Hoang |last2=Ris Lambers |first2=Janneke Hille |last3=Lutz |first3=James A. |last4=Metz |first4=Margaret |last5=Snell |first5=Rebecca S. |date=2024-04-08 |title=The importance of regeneration processes on forest biodiversity in old-growth forests in the Pacific Northwest |journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences |volume=379 |issue=1902 |article-number=20230016 |doi=10.1098/rstb.2023.0016 |pmid=38583471 |pmc=10999264 |bibcode=2024PTRSB.37930016L |issn=0962-8436}}</ref><ref name="Tree Death: Cause and Consequence"/> There are four stages to forest regrowth after a disturbance, the establishment phase which is rapid increase in seedlings, the thinning phase which happens after a canopy is formed and the seedlings covered by it die, the transition phase which occurs when one tree from the canopy dies and creates a pocket of light giving new seedlings opportunity to grow, and lastly the steady-state phase which happens when the forest has different sizes and ages of trees.<ref name="Tree Death: Cause and Consequence"/>

Christopherson. 1996</ref>

== Threats to forest ecology ==

=== Deforestation ===
A significant threat to forest ecology is deforestation as it removes large areas of forest for timer and land development.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Devaraju |first1=N. |last2=Bala |first2=Govindasamy |last3=Modak |first3=Angshuman |date=2015-03-17 |title=Effects of large-scale deforestation on precipitation in the monsoon regions: Remote versus local effects |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |language=en |volume=112 |issue=11 |pages=3257–3262 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1423439112 |doi-access=free |pmid=25733889 |pmc=4371945 |bibcode=2015PNAS..112.3257D |issn=0027-8424}}</ref><ref name=":6">{{Cite web |last1=Franklin |first1=Alan |last2=Noon |first2=Barry |last3=George |first3=Luke |date=2002 |title=What is Habitat Fragmentation? |url=https://digitalcommons.usf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1658&context=sab |access-date=2026-03-26 |website=Digital Sommons}}</ref> As trees are cleared, forest habitat become fragmented into smaller patches, making it harder for forest dependent species to fines resources like shelter, food, and mates.<ref>https://www.seesouthernforests.org/case-studies/biological-consequences-fragmentation/#:~:text=Fragmentation%20is%20problematic%20because%20it,invasive%20species%2C%20such%20as%20kudzu.</ref><ref name=":6" /> This poorly impacts forest ecology as it declines biodiversity and disrupts ecosystem functions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Magrach |first1=Ainhoa |last2=Senior |first2=Rebecca A. |last3=Rogers |first3=Andrew |last4=Nurdin |first4=Deddy |last5=Benedick |first5=Suzan |last6=Laurance |first6=William F. |last7=Santamaria |first7=Luis |last8=Edwards |first8=David P. |date=2016-03-16 |title=Selective logging in tropical forests decreases the robustness of liana–tree interaction networks to the loss of host tree species |journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences |language=en |volume=283 |issue=1826 |article-number=20153008 |doi=10.1098/rspb.2015.3008 |issn=0962-8452 |pmc=4810863 |pmid=26936241 |bibcode=2016PBioS.28353008M }}</ref> 

=== Urbanization and agriculture ===
Urbanization fragments habitats into roads, cities, and infrastructure development.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Faulkner |first=Stephen |date=2004-06-01 |title=Urbanization impacts on the structure and function of forested wetlands |journal=Urban Ecosystems |language=en |volume=7 |issue=2 |pages=89–106 |doi=10.1023/B:UECO.0000036269.56249.66 |bibcode=2004UrbEc...7...89F |issn=1573-1642}}</ref> This displaces wildlife and exposes forests to human disturbances. Likewise, agricultural activities transform forests into farmland and monocultures,<ref name=":6" /> introducing chemicals like fertilizers and pesticides that harm the soil.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Addison |first1=S. L. |last2=Smaill |first2=S. J. |last3=Garrett |first3=L. G. |last4=Wakelin |first4=S. A. |date=2021-07-01 |title=Fertiliser use has multi-decadal effects on microbial diversity and functionality of forest soils |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0929139321000858 |journal=Applied Soil Ecology |volume=163 |article-number=103964 |doi=10.1016/j.apsoil.2021.103964 |bibcode=2021AppSE.16303964A |issn=0929-1393}}</ref> This impacts forest ecology by altering nutrients cycles,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Guo |first1=Dali |last2=Mou |first2=Pu |last3=Jones |first3=Robert H. |last4=Mitchell |first4=Robert J. |date=2004-03-01 |title=Spatio-temporal patterns of soil available nutrients following experimental disturbance in a pine forest |journal=Oecologia |language=en |volume=138 |issue=4 |pages=613–621 |doi=10.1007/s00442-003-1473-3 |pmid=14689301 |issn=1432-1939}}</ref> degrading ecosystem health.  

=== Approaches ===
[[Image: Redwood M D Vaden.jpg|thumb|right|[[Sequoia sempervirens|Redwood]] tree in northern California forest, where many trees are managed for preservation and longevity]]
Forests are studied at a number of organizational levels, from the individual [[organism]] to the ecosystem. However, as the term [[forest]] connotes an area inhabited by more than one [[organism]], forest ecology most often concentrates on the level of the [[Population (biology)|population]], [[community]] or ecosystem. Logically, [[tree]]s are an important component of forest research, but the wide variety of other life forms and [[abiotic components]] in most forests means that other elements, such as [[wildlife]] or [[soil]] [[nutrients]], are also crucial components.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dunson |first1=William A. |last2=Travis |first2=Joseph |date=1991 |title=The Role of Abiotic Factors in Community Organization |journal=The American Naturalist |volume=138 |issue=5 |pages=1067–1091 |doi=10.1086/285270 |jstor=2462508 |bibcode=1991ANat..138.1067D |issn=0003-0147}}</ref>

Forest ecology shares characteristics and methodological approaches with other areas of [[terrestrial plant]] ecology, however, the presence of trees makes forest ecosystems and their study unique in numerous ways due to the potential for a wide variety of forest structures created by the uniquely large size and height of trees compared with other terrestrial plants.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ehbrecht |first1=Martin |last2=Seidel |first2=Dominik |last3=Annighöfer |first3=Peter |last4=Kreft |first4=Holger |last5=Köhler |first5=Michael |last6=Zemp |first6=Delphine Clara |last7=Puettmann |first7=Klaus |last8=Nilus |first8=Reuben |last9=Babweteera |first9=Fred |last10=Willim |first10=Katharina |last11=Stiers |first11=Melissa |last12=Soto |first12=Daniel |last13=Boehmer |first13=Hans Juergen |last14=Fisichelli |first14=Nicholas |last15=Burnett |first15=Michael |date=2021-01-22 |title=Global patterns and climatic controls of forest structural complexity |journal=Nature Communications |language=en |volume=12 |issue=1 |pages=519 |doi=10.1038/s41467-020-20767-z |pmid=33483481 |pmc=7822964 |bibcode=2021NatCo..12..519E |issn=2041-1723}}</ref>

The emergence of [[machine learning]](ML) has allowed for new methods of approaching forest ecology, as it can process larger and more complex data. Since the 1990s, machine learning is increasingly used to improve the accuracy of [[Species distribution modelling|species distribution models]], predict [[Carbon cycle|carbon flux]], and in hazard assessment procedures.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last1=Liu |first1=Zelin |last2=Peng |first2=Changhui |last3=Work |first3=Timothy |last4=Candau |first4=Jean-Noel |last5=DesRochers |first5=Annie |last6=Kneeshaw |first6=Daniel |date=2018 |title=Application of machine-learning methods in forest ecology: recent progress and future challenges |url=https://cdnsciencepub.com/doi/10.1139/er-2018-0034 |journal=Environmental Reviews |language=en |volume=26 |issue=4 |pages=339–350 |doi=10.1139/er-2018-0034 |bibcode=2018EnvRv..26..339L |hdl=1807/92561 |issn=1181-8700}}</ref> Drones are also heavily used in forest ecology research.<ref name=":5" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bygjymi |first1=Xhulia |last2=Begu |first2=Enkela |last3=Lloci |first3=Dritan |last4=Sinjari |first4=Sonila |last5=Hanxhari |first5=Romeo |date=2025 |title=The Use of Drone/Uav Technology in Precision Forestry. Case Study: National Park Divjake Karavasta |url=https://ijees.net/images/pdf/XhuliaBygjymi1EnkelaBegu1DritanLloci1SonilaSinjari1RomeoHanxhari1THEUSEOFDRONEUAVTECHNOLOGYINPRECISIONFORESTRYCASESTUDY:NATIONALPARKDIVJAKEKARAVASTApage103-108;-ab083755a2.pdf |journal=International Journal of Ecosystems and Ecology Sciences |volume=15 |issue=4 |pages=103–108 |doi=10.31407/ijees15.413 }}</ref>  The use of drones allows for easier mapping of forest landscapes, and surveying large sections of land. Using drones, information such as [[Tree height measurement|tree height]], diameter, species, and plant stress can be acquired with fewer expensive, labour intensive methods. They also aid in the identification of wildfires, especially when [[Drones in wildfire management|drones]] are equipped with [[Thermography|thermal cameras]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Buchelt |first1=Alexander |last2=Adrowitzer |first2=Alexander |last3=Kieseberg |first3=Peter |last4=Gollob |first4=Christoph |last5=Nothdurft |first5=Arne |last6=Eresheim |first6=Sebastian |last7=Tschiatschek |first7=Sebastian |last8=Stampfer |first8=Karl |last9=Holzinger |first9=Andreas |date=2024 |title=Exploring artificial intelligence for applications of drones in forest ecology and management |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0378112723007648 |journal=Forest Ecology and Management |language=en |volume=551 |article-number=121530 |doi=10.1016/j.foreco.2023.121530 |bibcode=2024ForEM.55121530B }}</ref>

=== Climate Change and Carbon Cycling ===
Climate change has an affect on forests from wildfires, droughts, soil erosion, and heat stress effects on vegetation.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Chapter 4 : Land Degradation — Special Report on Climate Change and Land|url=https://www.ipcc.ch/srccl/chapter/chapter-4/|access-date=2026-04-05}}</ref> The world resource institute summarizes the IPCC AR6 report and anthropogenic effects on global warming.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Boehm|first1=Sophie|last2=Schumer|first2=Clea|date=2023-03-20|title=10 Big Findings from the 2023 IPCC Report on Climate Change|url=https://www.wri.org/insights/2023-ipcc-ar6-synthesis-report-climate-change-findings|language=en}}</ref> The [[Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change|IPCC]] covers carbon removal and reforestation, the loss of vegetation impacts carbon cycling and effects vary among canopy structures . <ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Nave|first1=Lucas E.|last2=Gough|first2=Christopher M.|last3=Clay|first3=Cameron|last4=Santos|first4=Fernanda|last5=Atkins|first5=Jeff W.|last6=Benjamins-Carey|first6=Sonja E.|last7=Bohrer|first7=Gil|last8=Castillo|first8=Buck T.|last9=Fahey|first9=Robert T.|last10=Hardiman|first10=Brady S.|last11=Hofmeister|first11=Kathryn L.|last12=Ivanov|first12=Valeriy Y.|last13=Kalejs|first13=Jennifer|last14=Matheny|first14=Ashley M.|last15=Menna|first15=Angela C.|date=January 2025|title=Carbon cycling across ecosystem succession in a north temperate forest: Controls and management implications|url=https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/eap.70001|journal=Ecological Applications|language=en|volume=35|issue=1|article-number=e70001 |doi=10.1002/eap.70001|pmid=39989402 |bibcode=2025EcoAp..3570001N |osti=2538457 |issn=1051-0761|archive-url=http://web.archive.org/web/20250513002026/https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/eap.70001|archive-date=2025-05-13}}</ref>

=== Forest pathology ===
{{excerpt|Forest pathology}}

== Community diversity and complexity ==
[[File:Overall decline in a forest-specialist index for 268 forest vertebrate species (455 populations), 1970–2014.svg|thumb|upright=1.35|Overall decline in a forest-specialist index for 268 forest vertebrate species (455 populations), 1970–2014, from the [[Food and Agriculture Organization]] publication The State of the World's Forests 2020. Forests, biodiversity and people – In brief<ref>{{Cite book|title=The State of the World's Forests 2020. Forests, biodiversity and people – In brief|publisher=FAO & UNEP|year=2020|isbn=978-92-5-132707-4|location=Rome|doi=10.4060/ca8985en|s2cid=241416114}}</ref>]]
Since trees can grow larger than other plant life-forms, there is the potential for a wide variety of forest structures (or physiognomies). The infinite number of possible spatial arrangements of trees of varying size and species makes for a highly intricate and diverse micro-environment in which environmental variables such as [[solar radiation]], temperature, [[relative humidity]], and [[wind speed]] can vary considerably over large and small distances.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Schnabel |first1=Florian |last2=Beugnon |first2=Rémy |last3=Yang |first3=Bo |last4=Richter |first4=Ronny |last5=Eisenhauer |first5=Nico |last6=Huang |first6=Yuanyuan |last7=Liu |first7=Xiaojuan |last8=Wirth |first8=Christian |last9=Cesarz |first9=Simone |last10=Fichtner |first10=Andreas |last11=Perles-Garcia |first11=Maria D. |last12=Hähn |first12=Georg J. A. |last13=Härdtle |first13=Werner |last14=Kunz |first14=Matthias |last15=Castro Izaguirre |first15=Nadia C. |date=March 2025 |title=Tree Diversity Increases Forest Temperature Buffering via Enhancing Canopy Density and Structural Diversity |journal=Ecology Letters |volume=28 |issue=3 |pages=e70096 |doi=10.1111/ele.70096 |issn=1461-0248 |pmc=11928777 |pmid=40119529 |bibcode=2025EcolL..28E0096S }}</ref> In addition, an important proportion of a forest ecosystem's [[biomass (ecology)|biomass]] is often underground, where soil structure, [[water quality]] and quantity, and levels of various soil nutrients can vary greatly.<ref>James P. Kimmins. 2004</ref> Thus, forests are often highly [[heterogeneous]] environments compared to other [[terrestrial plant]] communities. This heterogeneity in turn can enable great biodiversity of species of both plants and animals. Some structures, such as tree ferns may be keystone species for a diverse range of other species.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Fountain-Jones | first1=Nicholas M. | last2=McQuillan | first2=Peter B. | last3=Grove | first3=Simon | title=Beetle communities associated with the tree fern ''Dicksonia antarctica'' Labill. In Tasmania | journal=Australian Journal of Entomology | date=2012 | volume=51 | issue=3 | pages=154–165 | doi=10.1111/j.1440-6055.2011.00855.x }}</ref>

A number of factors within the forest affect biodiversity; primary factors enhancing wildlife abundance and biodiversity was the presence of diverse tree species within the forest and the absence of [[even aged timber management]].<ref>Philip Joseph Burton. 2003</ref> For example, the [[wild turkey]] thrives when uneven heights and [[Canopy (biology)|canopy]] variations exist and its numbers are diminished by even aged timber management.

=== Tropical forests ===
[[File:Cuniculus_paca.jpg|thumb|Paca the South American rodent species that has shared features with the African chevrotain due to convergent evolution.]]
[[File:Indian_spotted_chevrotain_Moschiola_indica_Mouse_deer_from_the_Anaimalai_hills_DSC9927_03.jpg|thumb|The African chevrotain an ungulate that shares convergently evolved features with the South American paca.]]
[[Tropical forest|Tropical forests]] are some of the most [[Biodiversity|diverse]] ecosystems in the world.<ref name=":3">{{Cite book |last1=Ehrlich |first1=Paul R. |title=The science of ecology |last2=Roughgarden |first2=Joan |date=1987 |publisher=Macmillan ; Collier Macmillan |isbn=978-0-02-331700-2 |location=New York : London}}</ref> Although there are many different tree species present per acre of forest, many share similar appearances due to the similar environmental pressures.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite book |title=The International book of the forest |date=1981 |publisher=Simon and Schuster |isbn=978-0-671-41004-9 |location=New York}}</ref> Some of these shared traits, possessed by many tropical trees, include thick and leathery leaves that are elongated and ovular with [[Midrib|mid-ribs]] and [[Drip-tip|drip-tips]].<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":2" /> These adaptations help to quickly drain water from the leaves, likely to help prevent [[algae]] or [[lichen]] growth<ref name=":3" /> and prevent water reflecting the sunlight or restricting [[transpiration]].<ref name=":2" /> Commonly, tropical trees have large [[Buttress root|buttress roots]] on larger trees, and [[stilt roots]] on mid-sized trees which help support their tall and vertical structures in the shallow and moist soil.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":2" /> Tropical forests grow very densely due to the heavy rainfall and year-round growing season. This creates competition for light which causes many trees to grow very tall, blocking out most or all of the light from reaching the [[forest floor]].<ref name=":3" /> Because of this, the [[Canopy (biology)|canopy]] exhibits distinct stratified layers from the tallest trees to the tightly packed midstory trees below.<ref name=":3" /> Due to low light on the forest floor, there is a diverse population of [[Epiphyte|epiphytes]], a type of plant that grows on the canopy trees, rather than soil, to access better light. Many [[Vine|vines]] use a similar tactic, however they root in the ground, growing up the trees to reach light.<ref name=":3" /> The [[fauna]] in tropical forests also show many unique adaptations to fill various [[Ecological niche|niches]]. These adaptations are possessed by different species depending on where they are located.<ref name=":3" /> For example, there are similar looking animals in the rainforests of South America and Africa that share ecological niches, however the mammals from South America are [[Rodent|rodents]] while the African ones are [[Ungulate|ungulates]]. This clearly demonstrates the [[convergent evolution]] between species found in tropical forest environments.<ref name=":3" />

=== Coniferous forests ===
[[Conifer|Conifers]] have unique traits that make them especially adapted to harsh conditions, including cold, drought, wind, and snow.<ref name=":2" /> Their leaves have a [[wax]] coating and are filled with [[resin]] to help prevent moisture loss, this makes them unpalatable to animals and slow to [[Decomposition|decompose]]. This [[leaf litter]] creates an acidic forest floor that is distinct to coniferous forests.<ref name=":2" /> Because of the types of leaves possessed by conifers, they face the problem of soil nutrient loss; this problem is solved through [[Mycorrhizal network|mycorrhizal symbiosis]] with [[Fungus|fungi]] that help transport the limited nutrients to the trees in exchange for [[Glucose|sugars]].<ref name=":2" /> Some conifers are incapable of surviving without mycorrhizal fungi.<ref name=":2" /> The majority of conifers are also [[evergreen]], allowing them to take advantage of the short growing seasons of their respective environments.<ref name=":2" /> Their thin tapered structure helps them to withstand strong winds without being blown over.<ref name=":2" /> The stereotypically cone shape of conifers helps prevent large quantities of snow from building up on their branches and breaking them.<ref name=":3" /> Due to the harsh environments that coniferous forests are commonly found, the diversity is limited in both plant and animal species. The colder climates limit the number of [[Reptile|reptilian]] and [[amphibian]] species that can survive.<ref name=":2" /> The species more commonly found in coniferous forests are [[Mammal|mammals]], including large [[Herbivore|herbivores]] such as [[moose]] and [[elk]], [[Predation|predators]] like [[Bear|bears]] and [[Wolf|wolves]], along with a few smaller species like [[Rabbit|rabbits]], [[Fox|foxes]], and [[mink]]. There are also a variety of [[migratory bird]] species and some [[Bird of prey|birds of prey]] such as [[Owl|owls]] and [[Hawk|hawks]].<ref name=":2" /> Coniferous forests contain a variety of valuable [[Pulp (paper)|pulp]] and [[lumber]] trees making them some of the most [[economically]] important ecosystems.<ref name=":2" /> They have also been historically sought for the [[fur trade]] due to the animals species that inhabit them.<ref name=":2" />

== Ecological interactions ==

=== Plant-plant interactions ===
In forests, trees and shrubs often serve as [[nurse plants]] that facilitate the establishment and seedling growth of understory plants. The forest canopy protects young understory plants from extremes of temperature and dry conditions.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Martinkova |first1=Zdenka |last2=Honek |first2=Alois |last3=Pekar |first3=Stano |title=The Role of Nurse Plants in Facilitating the Germination of Dandelion (Taraxacum officinale) Seeds |journal=Weed Science |date=2014 |volume=62 |issue=3|pages=474–482 |doi=10.1614/WS-D-13-00162.1 |bibcode=2014WeedS..62..474M |s2cid=85658841 }}</ref>

=== Ecological potential of forest species ===
The ecological potential of a particular species is a measure of its capacity to effectively compete in a given geographical area, ahead of other species, as they all try to occupy a natural space. For some areas it has been quantified, as for instance by Hans-Jürgen Otto, for central Europe.<ref>{{cite book|last=Otto|first=Hans-Jürgen|title=Écologie Forestière|year=1998|publisher=Institut pour le Développement Forestier|location=Paris|isbn=978-2-904740-65-7|language=fr}}</ref> He takes three groups of parameters:

# Related to site requirements: Tolerance to low temperatures, tolerance to dry climate, frugality.
# Specific qualities: [[Shade tolerance]], height growth, stability, longevity, regeneration capacity.
# Specific risks: Resistance to late freezing, resistance to wind/ice storm, resistance to fire, resistance to biotic agents.

Every parameter is scored between 0 and 5 for each considered species, and then a global mean value calculated. A value above 3.5 is considered high, below 3.0 low, and intermediate for those in between. In this study ''[[Fagus sylvatica]]'' has a score of 3.82, ''[[Fraxinus excelsior]]'' 3.08 and ''[[Juglans regia]]'' 2.92; and are examples of the three categories.

=== Competition ===
Forest ecosystem interactions consist of not only symbiotic relationships, but also competition. Competition can either be in forms of [[Intraspecific competition|intraspecific]] or [[Interspecific competition|interspecific]] competition.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Interspecific Competition - an overview {{!}} ScienceDirect Topics|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/interspecific-competition|access-date=2026-04-05|website=www.sciencedirect.com}}</ref> Intraspecific competition can occur between members of the same species for resources, whereas interspecific competition occurs between different species in a population.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Interspecific Competition - an overview {{!}} ScienceDirect Topics|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/interspecific-competition|access-date=2026-04-05|website=www.sciencedirect.com}}</ref> For example, in order to fulfil nutritional needs decomposing organic matter in soils is a sought after resource by plants, microbes and fungi. <ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fontaine|first1=Sébastien|last2=Mariotti|first2=André|last3=Abbadie|first3=Luc|date=2003-06-01|title=The priming effect of organic matter: a question of microbial competition?|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0038071703001238|journal=Soil Biology and Biochemistry|volume=35|issue=6|pages=837–843|doi=10.1016/S0038-0717(03)00123-8|bibcode=2003SBiBi..35..837F |issn=0038-0717}}</ref> Invasive species in forest ecosystems also play a role in interspecific competition.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Invasive Species - an overview {{!}} ScienceDirect Topics|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/pharmacology-toxicology-and-pharmaceutical-science/invasive-species|access-date=2026-04-05|website=www.sciencedirect.com}}</ref> They often compete with native species for resources and may conquer these resources successfully due to low intraspecific competition.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Woo|first1=Sohyun|last2=Kim|first2=Tae-Min|last3=Kim|first3=Yousuk|last4=Jeong|first4=Seorin|last5=Kim|first5=Eunsuk|date=October 2024|title=Inter- and Intraspecific Competition in Invasive Lactuca serriola and Co-Occurring Weedy Plant Species|journal=Ecology and Evolution|volume=14|issue=10|pages=e70496|doi=10.1002/ece3.70496|issn=2045-7758|pmc=11522139|pmid=39478980 |bibcode=2024EcoEv..1470496W }}</ref> The [[hemlock woolly adelgid]] and the [[emerald ash borer]] are examples of well known invasive species that colonize an area and create disturbances in forest ecology by killing off host trees and decreasing the vegetation in a forest as a result.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Environmental and Ecological Impacts {{!}} National Invasive Species Information Center|url=https://www.invasivespeciesinfo.gov/subject/environmental-and-ecological-impacts|access-date=2026-04-05|website=www.invasivespeciesinfo.gov|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Canada|first=Natural Resources|date=2013-10-24|title=Emerald ash borer (factsheet)|url=https://natural-resources.canada.ca/forests-forestry/insects-disturbances/emerald-ash-borer-factsheet|access-date=2026-04-05|website=natural-resources.canada.ca}}</ref>

== Matter and energy flows ==

=== Energy flux ===
[[File:RockyPointTrailAsFirebreak.jpg|thumb|upright=1.1|Forest ecologists are interested in the effects of large disturbances, such as [[wildfire]]s. [[Montana]], United States.]]
Forests accumulate large amounts of standing biomass, and many are capable of accumulating it at high rates, i.e. they are highly productive. Such high levels of biomass and tall vertical structures represent large stores of [[potential energy]] that can be converted to [[kinetic energy]] under the right circumstances.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Running |first1=S. W. |title=Science |url=https://www.science.org/action/cookieAbsent |access-date=2026-03-30 |journal=Science |date=2008 |volume=321 |issue=5889 |pages=652–653 |language=en |doi=10.1126/science.1159607 |pmid=18669853 }}</ref>

The world's forests contain about 606 [[Metric ton|gigatonnes]] of living biomass (above- and below-ground) and 59 gigatonnes of dead wood.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Global Forest Resources Assessment 2020 – Key findings|publisher=FAO|year=2020|isbn=978-92-5-132581-0|location=Rome|doi=10.4060/ca8753en|s2cid=130116768}}</ref>

Two such conversions of great importance are [[wildfires|fires]] and [[windthrow|treefall]]s, both of which radically alter forest structure and ecosystem processes and the physical environment where they occur.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bowd |first1=Elle |last2=Lindenmayer |first2=David |date=January 2026 |title=Setting the benchmark: Patterns of forest structure after wildfire in temperate, montane forests across a multi-century chronosequence |url=https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1365-2745.70227 |journal=Journal of Ecology |language=en |volume=114 |issue=1 |article-number=e70227 |doi=10.1111/1365-2745.70227 |bibcode=2026JEcol.11470227B |issn=0022-0477}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Seidl |first1=Rupert |last2=Rammer |first2=Werner |last3=Spies |first3=Thomas A. |date=2014-12-01 |title=Disturbance legacies increase the resilience of forest ecosystem structure, composition, and functioning |journal=Ecological Applications: A Publication of the Ecological Society of America |volume=24 |issue=8 |pages=2063–2077 |doi=10.1890/14-0255.1 |issn=1051-0761 |pmc=4820056 |pmid=27053913 |bibcode=2014EcoAp..24.2063S }}</ref> Also, in forests of high productivity, the rapid growth of the trees themselves induces biome and environmental changes, although at a slower rate and lower intensity than relatively instantaneous [[disturbance (ecology)|disturbances]] such as fires.

=== Water ===
Forest trees store large amounts of water because of their large size and anatomical/physiological characteristics.  They are therefore important regulators of hydrological processes, especially those involving groundwater [[hydrology]] and local evaporation and [[Precipitation (meteorology)|rainfall/snowfall]] patterns.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Smerdon|first=Brian D|display-authors=etal|year=2009|title=An overview of the effects of forest management on ground water hydrology|url=http://forrex.org/sites/default/files/publications/jem_archive/ISS50/vol10_no1_art4.pdf|journal=BC Journal of Ecosystems and Management|volume=10|issue=1|pages=22–44|access-date=2016-11-21|archive-date=2016-11-22|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161122153621/http://forrex.org/sites/default/files/publications/jem_archive/ISS50/vol10_no1_art4.pdf}}</ref>

An estimated 399 million ha of forest is designated primarily for the protection of soil and water, an increase of 119 million ha since 1990.<ref name=":0" />

Thus, forest ecological studies are sometimes closely aligned with [[meteorology|meteorological]] and hydrological studies in regional ecosystem or resource planning studies. Perhaps more importantly the duff or [[leaf litter]] can form a major repository of water storage. When this litter is removed or compacted (through grazing or human overuse), erosion and flooding are exacerbated as well as deprivation of dry season water for forest organisms.

=== Death and regeneration ===
[[File:Cascades Regrowth after forest fire.jpg|thumb|upright=1.1|Forest regrowth after a forest fire, [[Cascade Range]], United States]]
Woody material, often referred to as [[coarse woody debris]], [[decomposition|decay]]s relatively slowly in many forests in comparison to most other [[organic matter|organic]] materials, due to a combination of environmental factors and wood chemistry (see [[lignin]]).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ganjegunte |first1=Girisha K |last2=Condron |first2=Leo M |last3=Clinton |first3=Peter W |last4=Davis |first4=Murray R |last5=Mahieu |first5=Nathalie |date=2004-01-23 |title=Decomposition and nutrient release from radiata pine (Pinus radiata) coarse woody debris |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378112703003323 |journal=Forest Ecology and Management |language=en |volume=187 |issue=2 |pages=197–211 |doi=10.1016/S0378-1127(03)00332-3 |bibcode=2004ForEM.187..197G |issn=0378-1127|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Trees growing in [[arid]] and/or cold environments do so especially slowly. Thus, tree trunks and branches can remain on the [[forest floor]] for long periods, affecting such things as wildlife [[habitat]], fire behaviour, and tree [[regeneration (biology)|regeneration]] processes.

Some trees leave behind eerie skeletons after death. In reality these deaths are actually very few compared to the amount of tree deaths that go unnoticed. Thousands of seedlings can be produced from a single tree but only a few can actually grow to maturity.<ref name="Tree Death: Cause and Consequence">{{Cite journal|date=1987|title=Competition and Tree Death|journal=BioScience |volume=37|pages=586–595|jstor=1310669|last1=Peet|first1=Robert K.|last2=Christensen|first2=Norman L.|issue=8|doi=10.2307/1310669}}</ref> Most of those deaths are caused from competition for light, water, or soil nutrients, this is called natural thinning. Singular deaths caused by natural thinning go unnoticed, but many deaths can help form forest ecosystems.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Swanson |first1=Mark E |last2=Franklin |first2=Jerry F |last3=Beschta |first3=Robert L |last4=Crisafulli |first4=Charles M |last5=DellaSala |first5=Dominick A |last6=Hutto |first6=Richard L |last7=Lindenmayer |first7=David B |last8=Swanson |first8=Frederick J |date=2011 |title=The forgotten stage of forest succession: early-successional ecosystems on forest sites |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1890/090157 |journal=Frontiers in Ecology and the Environment |language=en |volume=9 |issue=2 |pages=117–125 |doi=10.1890/090157 |bibcode=2011FrEE....9..117S |issn=1540-9309}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Luu |first1=Hoang |last2=Ris Lambers |first2=Janneke Hille |last3=Lutz |first3=James A. |last4=Metz |first4=Margaret |last5=Snell |first5=Rebecca S. |date=2024-04-08 |title=The importance of regeneration processes on forest biodiversity in old-growth forests in the Pacific Northwest |journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences |volume=379 |issue=1902 |article-number=20230016 |doi=10.1098/rstb.2023.0016 |pmid=38583471 |pmc=10999264 |bibcode=2024PTRSB.37930016L |issn=0962-8436}}</ref><ref name="Tree Death: Cause and Consequence"/> There are four stages to forest regrowth after a disturbance, the establishment phase which is rapid increase in seedlings, the thinning phase which happens after a canopy is formed and the seedlings covered by it die, the transition phase which occurs when one tree from the canopy dies and creates a pocket of light giving new seedlings opportunity to grow, and lastly the steady-state phase which happens when the forest has different sizes and ages of trees.<ref name="Tree Death: Cause and Consequence"/>

[[Image:Daintree Rainforest.JPG|thumb|right|The [[Daintree Rainforest]] in [[Queensland]], Australia]]
'''Forest ecology''' is the scientific study of the interrelated patterns, processes, [[flora]], [[fauna]], [[funga]], and [[ecosystem]]s in [[forests]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Führer |first=Erwin |date=2000-06-15 |title=Forest functions, ecosystem stability and management |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378112700003777 |journal=Forest Ecology and Management |language=en |volume=132 |issue=1 |pages=29–38 |doi=10.1016/S0378-1127(00)00377-7 |bibcode=2000ForEM.132...29F |issn=0378-1127|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The management of forests is known as [[forestry]], [[silviculture]], and [[forest management]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bauhus |first1=Jürgen |last2=Puettmann |first2=Klaus |last3=Messier |first3=Christian |date=2009-07-30 |title=Silviculture for old-growth attributes |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378112709000905 |journal=Forest Ecology and Management |series=Old forests, new management: the conservation and use of old-growth forests in the 21st century |volume=258 |issue=4 |pages=525–537 |doi=10.1016/j.foreco.2009.01.053 |bibcode=2009ForEM.258..525B |issn=0378-1127|url-access=subscription }}</ref> A forest [[ecosystem]] is a natural woodland unit consisting of all plants, animals, and micro-organisms ([[biotic component]]s) in that area functioning together with all of the non-living physical ([[abiotic]]) factors of the environment.<ref>Robert W. Christopherson. 1996</ref>

== Importance ==
Forests have an enormously important role to play in the [[Biosphere|global ecosystem]], as they cover almost a third of all land.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Schmitt |first1=Christine B. |last2=Burgess |first2=Neil D. |last3=Coad |first3=Lauren |last4=Belokurov |first4=Alexander |last5=Besançon |first5=Charles |last6=Boisrobert |first6=Lauriane |last7=Campbell |first7=Alison |last8=Fish |first8=Lucy |last9=Gliddon |first9=Derek |last10=Humphries |first10=Kate |last11=Kapos |first11=Valerie |last12=Loucks |first12=Colby |last13=Lysenko |first13=Igor |last14=Miles |first14=Lera |last15=Mills |first15=Craig |date=2009 |title=Global analysis of the protection status of the world's forests |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0006320709001943 |journal=Biological Conservation being created by oceanic plankton),<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nationalgeographic.org/activity/save-the-plankton-breathe-freely/|title = Save the Plankton, Breathe Freely|date = 28 February 2012}}</ref> and serve as crucial carbon sinks.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Phillips |first1=Oliver L. |last2=Malhi |first2=Yadvinder |last3=Higuchi |first3=Niro |last4=Laurance |first4=William F. |last5=Núñez |first5=Percy V. |last6=Vásquez |first6=Rodolfo M. |last7=Laurance |first7=Susan G. |last8=Ferreira |first8=Leandro V. |last9=Stern |first9=Margaret |last10=Brown |first10=Sandra |last11=Grace |first11=John |date=1998-10-16 |title=Changes in the Carbon Balance of Tropical Forests: Evidence from Long-Term Plots |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.282.5388.439 |journal=Science |volume=282 |issue=5388 |pages=439–442 |doi=10.1126/science.282.5388.439 |pmid=9774263 |bibcode=1998Sci...282..439P }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Sedjo |first1=Roger |last2=Sohngen |first2=Brent |date=2012-08-01 |title=Carbon Sequestration in Forests and Soils |url=https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-resource-083110-115941 through a [[biotic pump]], which draws moisture from the ocean in order to replace natural water losses.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Makarieva |first1=A. Case Study: Krupanj Municipality—Serbia |journal=Forests |language=en |volume=14 |issue=6 |page=1127 |doi=10.3390/f14061127  |doi-access=free|bibcode=2023Fore...14.1127B |issn=1999-4907}}</ref> Forests also host 80% of all terrestrial organisms.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Leuschner |first1=C. |title=Global Forest Biodiversity: Current State, Trends, and Threats |date=2023 |work=Progress in Botany Vol. 83 |pages=125–159 |editor-last=Lüttge |editor-first=Ulrich  |place=Cham |publisher=Springer International Publishing |language=en |doi=10.1007/124_2022_58 |isbn=978-3-031-12782-3 |last2=Homeier |first2=J. |editor2-last=Cánovas |editor2-first=Francisco M. |editor3-last=Risueño |editor3-first=María-Carmen |editor4-last=Leuschner |editor4-first=Christoph}}</ref> and provide services for humans as well. == Threats to forest ecology ==

=== Deforestation ===
A significant threat to forest ecology is deforestation as it removes large areas of forest for timer and land development.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Devaraju |first1=N. |last2=Bala |first2=Govindasamy |last3=Modak |first3=Angshuman |date=2015-03-17 |title=Effects of large-scale deforestation on precipitation in the monsoon regions: Remote versus local effects |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |language=en |volume=112 |issue=11 |pages=3257–3262 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1423439112 |doi-access=free |pmid=25733889 |pmc=4371945 |bibcode=2015PNAS..112.3257D |issn=0027-8424}}</ref><ref name=":6">{{Cite web |last1=Franklin |first1=Alan |last2=Noon |first2=Barry |last3=George |first3=Luke |date=2002 |title=What is Habitat Fragmentation? |url=https://digitalcommons.usf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1658&context=sab |access-date=2026-03-26 |website=Digital Sommons}}</ref> As trees are cleared, forest habitat become fragmented into smaller patches, making it harder for forest dependent species to fines resources like shelter, food, and mates.<ref>https://www.seesouthernforests.org/case-studies/biological-consequences-fragmentation/#:~:text=Fragmentation%20is%20problematic%20because%20it,invasive%20species%2C%20such%20as%20kudzu.</ref><ref name=":6" /> This poorly impacts forest ecology as it declines biodiversity and disrupts ecosystem functions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Magrach |first1=Ainhoa |last2=Senior |first2=Rebecca A. |last3=Rogers |first3=Andrew |last4=Nurdin |first4=Deddy |last5=Benedick |first5=Suzan |last6=Laurance |first6=William F. |last7=Santamaria |first7=Luis |last8=Edwards |first8=David P. |date=2016-03-16 |title=Selective logging in tropical forests decreases the robustness of liana–tree interaction networks to the loss of host tree species |journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences |language=en |volume=283 |issue=1826 |article-number=20153008 |doi=10.1098/rspb.2015.3008 |issn=0962-8452 |pmc=4810863 |pmid=26936241 |bibcode=2016PBioS.28353008M }}</ref> 

=== Urbanization and agriculture ===
Urbanization fragments habitats into roads, cities, and infrastructure development.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Faulkner |first=Stephen |date=2004-06-01 |title=Urbanization impacts on the structure and function of forested wetlands |journal=Urban Ecosystems |language=en |volume=7 |issue=2 |pages=89–106 |doi=10.1023/B:UECO.0000036269.56249.66 |bibcode=2004UrbEc...7...89F |issn=1573-1642}}</ref> This displaces wildlife and exposes forests to human disturbances. Likewise, agricultural activities transform forests into farmland and monocultures,<ref name=":6" /> introducing chemicals like fertilizers and pesticides that harm the soil.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Addison |first1=S. L. |last2=Smaill |first2=S. J. |last3=Garrett |first3=L. G. |last4=Wakelin |first4=S. A. |date=2021-07-01 |title=Fertiliser use has multi-decadal effects on microbial diversity and functionality of forest soils |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0929139321000858 |journal=Applied Soil Ecology |volume=163 |article-number=103964 |doi=10.1016/j.apsoil.2021.103964 |bibcode=2021AppSE.16303964A |issn=0929-1393}}</ref> This impacts forest ecology by altering nutrients cycles,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Guo |first1=Dali |last2=Mou |first2=Pu |last3=Jones |first3=Robert H. |last4=Mitchell |first4=Robert J. |date=2004-03-01 |title=Spatio-temporal patterns of soil available nutrients following experimental disturbance in a pine forest |journal=Oecologia |language=en |volume=138 |issue=4 |pages=613–621 |doi=10.1007/s00442-003-1473-3 |pmid=14689301 |issn=1432-1939}}</ref> degrading ecosystem health.  

=== Approaches ===
[[Image: Redwood M D Vaden.jpg|thumb|right|[[Sequoia sempervirens|Redwood]] tree in northern California forest, where many trees are managed for preservation and longevity]]
Forests are studied at a number of organizational levels, from the individual [[organism]] to the ecosystem. However, as the term [[forest]] connotes an area inhabited by more than one [[organism]], forest ecology most often concentrates on the level of the [[population]], [[community]] or ecosystem. Logically, [[tree]]s are an important component of forest research, but the wide variety of other life forms and [[abiotic components]] in most forests means that other elements, such as [[wildlife]] or [[soil]] [[nutrients]], are also crucial components.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dunson |first1=William A. |last2=Travis |first2=Joseph |date=1991 |title=The Role of Abiotic Factors in Community Organization |journal=The American Naturalist |volume=138 |issue=5 |pages=1067–1091 |doi=10.1086/285270 |jstor=2462508 |bibcode=1991ANat..138.1067D |issn=0003-0147}}</ref>

Forest ecology shares characteristics and methodological approaches with other areas of [[terrestrial plant]] ecology, however, the presence of trees makes forest ecosystems and their study unique in numerous ways due to the potential for a wide variety of forest structures created by the uniquely large size and height of trees compared with other terrestrial plants.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ehbrecht |first1=Martin |last2=Seidel |first2=Dominik |last3=Annighöfer |first3=Peter |last4=Kreft |first4=Holger |last5=Köhler |first5=Michael |last6=Zemp |first6=Delphine Clara |last7=Puettmann |first7=Klaus |last8=Nilus |first8=Reuben |last9=Babweteera |first9=Fred |last10=Willim |first10=Katharina |last11=Stiers |first11=Melissa |last12=Soto |first12=Daniel |last13=Boehmer |first13=Hans Juergen |last14=Fisichelli |first14=Nicholas |last15=Burnett |first15=Michael |date=2021-01-22 |title=Global patterns and climatic controls of forest structural complexity |journal=Nature Communications |language=en |volume=12 |issue=1 |pages=519 |doi=10.1038/s41467-020-20767-z |pmid=33483481 |pmc=7822964 |bibcode=2021NatCo..12..519E |issn=2041-1723}}</ref>

The emergence of [[machine learning]](ML) has allowed for new methods of approaching forest ecology, as it can process larger and more complex data. === Climate Change and Carbon Cycling ===

== Community diversity and complexity ==
[[File:Overall decline in a forest-specialist index for 268 forest vertebrate species (455 populations), 1970–2014.svg|thumb|upright=1.35|Overall decline in a forest-specialist index for 268 forest vertebrate species (455 populations), 1970–2014, from the [[Food and Agriculture Organization]] publication The State of the World's Forests 2020. Forests, biodiversity and people – In brief<ref>{{Cite book|title=The State of the World's Forests 2020. Forests, biodiversity and people – In brief|publisher=FAO & UNEP|year=2020|isbn=978-92-5-132707-4|location=Rome|doi=10.4060/ca8985en|s2cid=241416114}}</ref>]]
Since trees can grow larger than other plant life-forms, there is the potential for a wide variety of forest structures (or physiognomies). The infinite number of possible spatial arrangements of trees of varying size and species makes for a highly intricate and diverse micro-environment in which environmental variables such as [[solar radiation]], temperature, [[relative humidity]], and [[wind speed]] can vary considerably over large and small distances.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Schnabel |first1=Florian |last2=Beugnon |first2=Rémy |last3=Yang |first3=Bo |last4=Richter |first4=Ronny |last5=Eisenhauer |first5=Nico |last6=Huang |first6=Yuanyuan |last7=Liu |first7=Xiaojuan |last8=Wirth |first8=Christian |last9=Cesarz |first9=Simone |last10=Fichtner |first10=Andreas |last11=Perles-Garcia |first11=Maria D. |last12=Hähn |first12=Georg J. A. |last13=Härdtle |first13=Werner |last14=Kunz |first14=Matthias |last15=Castro Izaguirre |first15=Nadia C. |date=March 2025 |title=Tree Diversity Increases Forest Temperature Buffering via Enhancing Canopy Density and Structural Diversity |journal=Ecology Letters |volume=28 |issue=3 |pages=e70096 |doi=10.1111/ele.70096 |issn=1461-0248 |pmc=11928777 |pmid=40119529 |bibcode=2025EcolL..28E0096S }}</ref> In addition, an important proportion of a forest ecosystem's [[biomass (ecology)|biomass]] is often underground, where soil structure, [[water quality]] and quantity, and levels of various soil nutrients can vary greatly.<ref>James P. Kimmins. 2004</ref> Thus, forests are often highly [[heterogeneous]] environments compared to other [[terrestrial plant]] communities. This heterogeneity in turn can enable great biodiversity of species of both plants and animals. Some structures, such as tree ferns may be keystone species for a diverse range of other species.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Fountain-Jones | first1=Nicholas M. | last2=McQuillan | first2=Peter B. | last3=Grove | first3=Simon | title=Beetle communities associated with the tree fern ''Dicksonia antarctica'' Labill. In Tasmania | journal=Australian Journal of Entomology | date=2012 | volume=51 | issue=3 | pages=154–165 | doi=10.1111/j.1440-6055.2011.00855.x }}</ref>

A number of factors within the forest affect biodiversity; primary factors enhancing wildlife abundance and biodiversity was the presence of diverse tree species within the forest and the absence of [[even aged timber management]].<ref>Philip Joseph Burton. 2003</ref> For example, the [[wild turkey]] thrives when uneven heights and [[Canopy (biology)|canopy]] variations exist and its numbers are diminished by even aged timber management.

Forest management techniques that mimic natural disturbance events<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Putz |first1=Francis E |last2=Romero |first2=Claudia |last3=Sist |first3=Plinio |last4=Schwartz |first4=Gustavo |last5=Thompson |first5=Ian |last6=Roopsind |first6=Anand |last7=Ruslandi |last8=Medjibe |first8=Vincent |last9=Ellis |first9=Peter |date=2022-07-01 |editor-last=Bayer |editor-first=Edward |title=Sustained timber yield claims, considerations, and tradeoffs for selectively logged forests |url=https://academic.oup.com/pnasnexus/article/doi/10.1093/pnasnexus/pgac102/6625051 |journal=PNAS Nexus |language=en |volume=1 |issue=3 |article-number=pgac102 |doi=10.1093/pnasnexus/pgac102 |doi-access=free |issn=2752-6542 |pmc=10468026 |pmid=37654970}}</ref> (variable retention forestry<ref>Franklin et al 1997</ref>) can allow community diversity to recover rapidly for a variety of groups including beetles.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Fountain-Jones | first1=Nicholas M. | last2=Baker | first2=Susan C. | last3=Jordan | first3=Gregory J. | title=Moving beyond the guild concept: Developing a practical functional trait framework for terrestrial beetles | journal=Ecological Entomology | date=2015 | volume=40 | issue=1 | pages=1–13 | doi=10.1111/een.12158 | bibcode=2015EcoEn..40....1F | url=https://figshare.com/articles/journal_contribution/22921565 }}</ref>
